content: Cervicitis refers to the inflammation of the cervical tissues. It can be classified based on its cause, anatomical location, and duration, such as infectious or non-infectious, and acute, subacute, or chronic. The most common infectious causes are Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It is important to distinguish cervicitis from other conditions that may cause similar symptoms, such as endometritis, salpingitis, vaginitis, or vulvovaginitis. Mucopurulent cervicitis is often asymptomatic, but some patients may experience abnormal vaginal discharge, pain during sexual intercourse, or bleeding between menstrual periods. Risk factors for cervicitis include high-risk sexual behaviors, a history of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), early sexual activity, multiple sexual partners, low socioeconomic status, smoking, alcohol or drug use, and bacterial vaginosis. There is no single definitive diagnostic test for cervicitis. Two key diagnostic signs are the presence of purulent or mucopurulent endocervical discharge visible in the cervical canal or on a swab, and easily induced endocervical bleeding when a cotton swab is gently passed through the cervical os. A clinical diagnosis is often made, but laboratory findings such as more than 10 white blood cells (WBCs) in vaginal fluid, in the absence of trichomoniasis, may indicate endocervical inflammation caused by C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae. Cultures are more accurate for diagnosing gonococcal cervicitis. Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are highly sensitive for detecting trichomoniasis, while wet mount microscopy has low sensitivity for N. gonorrhoeae and Trichomonas vaginalis. Testing for herpes simplex virus (HSV-2) is not routinely recommended for cervicitis diagnosis. If left untreated, cervicitis can lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), infertility, chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, spontaneous abortion, premature rupture of membranes, and preterm delivery. In cases of untreated active HSV infections during the perinatal or neonatal period, neonatal morbidity may occur. The recommended treatment for cervicitis includes antimicrobial therapy targeting C. trachomatis. The first-line regimen is doxycycline 100 mg taken orally twice daily for seven days. An alternative is a single dose of azithromycin 1 g taken orally. If N. gonorrhoeae is suspected, concomitant therapy is required. Sexual partners should also be treated to prevent reinfection. Follow-up after completing the antimicrobial regimen is necessary to assess for microbial resistance. Cervicitis can be caused by both infectious and non-infectious factors. Infectious causes include C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, T. vaginalis, HSV-2, and Mycoplasma genitalium. The pathophysiology of cervicitis varies depending on the causative agent. For example, N. gonorrhoeae infects the cervix through type IV pilus-mediated motility, which is enhanced in the presence of seminal fluid. This leads to local inflammation and purulent discharge. C. trachomatis infection triggers intense lymphocytic and neutrophilic inflammation, sometimes with follicular lymphocyte aggregation. Chronic chlamydial cervicitis is associated with low levels of cytokines such as IL-1α, IL-1β, and TNFα, but elevated IL-8 levels. The prevalence of cervicitis varies by population. It is more common in women with HIV and in underserved communities. Chlamydial cervicitis is four to five times more prevalent than gonococcal cervicitis. Co-infection with both pathogens is more common in PID than in cervicitis. Cervicitis is most frequently diagnosed in women aged 15–24 years, with no racial predilection. Screening for infectious causes of cervicitis is recommended for sexually active women under 25 years of age, women aged 25 and older at increased risk, and all pregnant women at risk. Early diagnosis and treatment of STIs, particularly gonorrhea and chlamydia, are essential for secondary prevention. Imaging studies such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and ultrasounds are not typically used to diagnose cervicitis. However, ultrasound may be helpful if cervicitis is complicated by PID. Surgical intervention is not required for cervicitis management. Primary prevention strategies include reducing risk factors such as high-risk sexual behaviors and ensuring safe sexual practices. Secondary prevention involves early detection and treatment of STIs to prevent complications.
